Ladies and gentlemen, rap is no longer dominating the charts. Upon looking at the top 20 of the billboard hot 100, only 1 rap song is currently on the chart. Upon viewing the remaining 80 artists, the vast majority of them are a mix of pop, country, Latino among others. There are still a handful of rappers sprinkled throughout the list but by far dominated by other genres compared to 10-15 years ago. This begs the age old question. Is rap finally reaching its slow demise from the mainstream spotlight? Is rap slowly but surely returning to the underground much like rock and roll? To compare trajectories, rock and roll reached its peak during the golden era of the 1960is and then died a very slow death in the following 3 decades. By the mid 90is rock was already being replaced by hip hop/r&b on the mainstream charts and was fully dominated by the early-mid 2000is. If we look at the similar trend of rap/hip hop, the 90is was considered the golden era. This was rapis ??960is??so to speak. In 2026 we are now in the middle of the 3rd decade since the domination of rap much like the 1990is for rock, where we are now seeing a slow shifting trend in popularity. Perhaps toward Latino genres? Maybe country? Love to hear your thoughts.

I agree, I'm a 26 y/o straight guy so I'm not the target audience but I do enjoy the music of other pop girls. I went through a phase of listening to The Subway on repeat. But with Sabrina I just don't get it. The music is bland, there's no distinct sound like Olivia's pop-punk guitar edge and the hooks aren't particularly memorable. Espresso aside, I couldn't hum another Sabrina Carpenter song and I've definitely heard some. I also find the overtly sexual lyrics a bit icky especially considering how many teenage and preteen fans she has. It's better than the misogyny in 00's hip-hop I suppose. With her image, yes it's very manufactured, but who is it for? On stage she dresses in a very male-gaze-y way, I mean she can wear what she wants but I don't get it.

She creates very catchy pop songs with impeccable pop production, loads up her lyrics with self-depricating humor as well as double entendres, and writes from the very relatable POV of a straight woman who desires a fullfilling relationship from a man, but is willing to settle for sex because the men she encounters in her songs end up disappointing her in one way or another. Her whole image is definitely rooted in drag, which is an extreme exaggeration of femininity, and she draws upon pop, rock and country sounds in her music. On her new record, you can hear nods to Shania Twain, TLC, En Vogue, ABBA, Dolly Parton, and probably a lot more. It's like drinking a McDonald's Coke. Everything from the syrup:soda ratio to the size of the straw, to the texture of the ice, to the design of the cup, to the design of the lid, has been carefully considered, calibrated, and executed to make you feel good, and make you want more, which is the classic pop music formula. She's doing it better than most right now.

Pop, country & rnb are the big genres in US right now, but the US is not where cool new music is being made right now. I'd look at UK to see where the game is at. Amapiano had a small moment, I'll think we'll see some integration in the mainstream (Central Cee already had some of those vibes on his songs). Garage is going mainstream, Interplanetary Criminal is doing dope stuff. Dnb is also growing. But also more analog punk stuff to counteract the AI and everything being polished. Internet Girl and Yungblud are two that I follow. What I think will happen is that none of these trends are monolithic enough to become the mainstream on their own. However I think we'll see elements of all of these integrated into the mainstream as flavors. What Dua Lipa did to disco and what The Weekend did to synthpop will probably happen to these genres also.
